    The model bench: open and closed boxes

    Raban Heller, Gerhard Achatz

    Source: vignettes/model-bench.Rmd
    model-bench.Rmd
    library(sandtablR)

    An interpretable model is worth having only if you know what it costs. This article measures that: the same data, the same preprocessing, the same held-out split, scored across engines you can read and engines you cannot.

    The modelling chunks require parsnip, recipes, workflows, rsample, tune, yardstick, dials, hardhat, rpart, glmnet and ranger. The explanation chunks additionally require DALEX and DALEXtra. Sections with missing optional packages are not executed; the table below records which parts are available in this build.

    data.frame(section = c("Model comparison", "Explanations"),
           available = c(bench_ready, explain_ready))
#>            section available
#> 1 Model comparison      TRUE
#> 2     Explanations      TRUE

    Define the target before comparing models

    The first thing to get right is what to predict.

    The card’s true sighting category is a deterministic function of life points by construction: red is 1–4, yellow 5–8, green 9–12. Any engine recovers that rule exactly, so a leaderboard on it is a row of ones.

    co <- sdt_synthetic_cohort(n = 400, seed = 1)
trivial <- sdt_fit(co, target = "triage", engine = "tree",
                   tune = FALSE, folds = 3, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
sdt_metrics(trivial)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   .metric  .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>    <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 accuracy multiclass         1
#> 2 f_meas   macro              1
#> 3 kap      multiclass         1
#> 4 roc_auc  hand_till          1

    What a participant calls is a different matter. The published evaluation reports how often participants agreed with the card: 88% for red, 59% for yellow, 71% for green. sdt_add_decisions() generates calls with those hit rates, weighting miscalls toward neighbouring categories, since red is mistaken for yellow far more often than for green.

    labelled <- sdt_add_decisions(sdt_synthetic_cohort(n = 800, seed = 5),
                              seed = 6)
table(true = labelled$triage, called = labelled$called_triage)
#>         called
#> true     green red yellow
#>   green    166  27     46
#>   red       13 318     31
#>   yellow    45  34    120

    Agreement between the two is well above chance and well short of perfect, which is what makes it a real prediction problem:

    sdt_consistency_score(labelled$triage, labelled$called_triage)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate     n
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl> <int>
#> 1 kap     multiclass     0.618   800

    Kappa accounts for agreement expected from the marginal category frequencies. Raw agreement alone can look high when one category dominates. If both raters always choose the same category, agreement is 100% but kappa is undefined; there is no variation with which to assess discrimination.

    The bench

    sdt_workflowset() fits every installed engine to the same data through the same recipe and returns one leaderboard. Engines whose package is missing are skipped and named, not silently dropped.

    board <- sdt_workflowset(
  labelled, target = "called_triage",
  engines = c("tree", "glmnet", "ranger"),
  tune = FALSE, folds = 3, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE
)
board
#> # A tibble: 12 × 5
#>    engine class_box .metric  .estimator .estimate
#>    <chr>  <chr>     <chr>    <chr>          <dbl>
#>  1 tree   glass     accuracy multiclass     0.776
#>  2 tree   glass     f_meas   macro          0.746
#>  3 tree   glass     kap      multiclass     0.651
#>  4 tree   glass     roc_auc  hand_till      0.841
#>  5 ranger black     accuracy multiclass     0.746
#>  6 ranger black     f_meas   macro          0.700
#>  7 ranger black     kap      multiclass     0.600
#>  8 ranger black     roc_auc  hand_till      0.817
#>  9 glmnet glass     accuracy multiclass     0.692
#> 10 glmnet glass     f_meas   macro          0.603
#> 11 glmnet glass     kap      multiclass     0.495
#> 12 glmnet glass     roc_auc  hand_till      0.809

    class_box is the column the article is about. glass marks models whose decision rule can be read off directly: a single decision tree, a penalised multinomial regression. black marks models that cannot be, however good.

    attr(board, "skipped")
#> character(0)

    The fitted models come back attached, so the winner can be interrogated without refitting:

    models <- attr(board, "models")
names(models)
#> [1] "tree"   "glmnet" "ranger"

    Read the comparison

    The question is not which engine wins. It is how much is given up by choosing one you can read.

    auc <- board[board$.metric == "roc_auc", ]
glass <- max(auc$.estimate[auc$class_box == "glass"])
black <- max(auc$.estimate[auc$class_box == "black"])
c(best_glass_box = glass, best_black_box = black, difference = glass - black)
#> best_glass_box best_black_box     difference 
#>     0.84145363     0.81741541     0.02403822

    The printed gap describes this synthetic sample, split and set of fixed hyperparameters. Its sign and size are outcomes of the example, not a general claim that one model family is superior. Selecting the best engine using this comparison also requires a separate final evaluation for an unbiased assessment.

    best <- auc$engine[which.max(auc$.estimate)]
sdt_roc(models[[best]])

    ROC curves, one per class, for the leading model. Synthetic demonstration.

    Explaining both the same way

    A glass-box model can be read directly, but a black-box one cannot, so the only way to put them side by side is to explain both from the outside. Permutation importance does that: it asks how much worse a model gets when a predictor is shuffled, which is defined identically for every engine.

    sdt_importance(models[[best]], n_permutations = 5)

    Permutation variable importance for the leading model. Synthetic demonstration.

    Agreement between importance profiles does not establish a causal explanation. Correlated predictors, model instability and the evaluation sample can affect these summaries. Inspect the predictive results and the data-generating assumptions alongside each explanation.

    sdt_profile(models[[best]], variables = "life_points")

    Partial dependence of predicted probability on life points. Synthetic demonstration.

    For a single casualty, sdt_shap() decomposes one prediction into per-predictor contributions: not “what does this model use”, but “why this casualty”.

    Caveats

    Everything above runs on synthetic data whose structure is known, because it was generated. That is useful for demonstrating the bench and useless as evidence about real mass-casualty decision-making. With a real seed cohort, sdt_synthesise() produces a synthetic candidate and sdt_synthesis_utility() assesses utility. Neither establishes anonymity or permission to release data; privacy assessment and disclosure review are separate tasks.
